# On Overfitting and Asymptotic Bias in Batch Reinforcement Learning with Partial Observability

## Article Sidebar

[PDF](https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11478/26494)

**Published:** May 5, 2019 

**DOI:**[https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.11478](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.11478)

**Keywords:**

 reinforcement learning, machine learning, knowledge representation 

## Main Article Content

**Vincent Francois-Lavet**

**Guillaume Rabusseau**

**Joelle Pineau**

**Damien Ernst**

**Raphael Fonteneau**

## Abstract

This paper provides an analysis of the tradeoff between asymptotic bias (suboptimality with unlimited data) and overfitting (additional suboptimality due to limited data) in the context of reinforcement learning with partial observability.Our theoretical analysis formally characterizes that while potentially increasing the asymptotic bias, a smaller state representation decreases the risk of overfitting.This analysis relies on expressing the quality of a state representation by bounding $L_1$ error terms of the associated belief states.Theoretical results are empirically illustrated when the state representation is a truncated history of observations, both on synthetic POMDPs and on a large-scale POMDP in the context of smartgrids, with real-world data.Finally, similarly to known results in the fully observable setting, we also briefly discuss and empirically illustrate how using function approximators and adapting the discount factor may enhance the tradeoff between asymptotic bias and overfitting in the partially observable context.

# On Overfitting and Asymptotic Bias in Batch Reinforcement Learning with Partial Observability

## Article Sidebar

[PDF](https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11478/26494)

**Published:** May 5, 2019 

**DOI:**[https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.11478](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.11478)

**Keywords:**

 reinforcement learning, machine learning, knowledge representation 

## Main Article Content

**Vincent Francois-Lavet**

**Guillaume Rabusseau**

**Joelle Pineau**

**Damien Ernst**

**Raphael Fonteneau**

## Abstract

This paper provides an analysis of the tradeoff between asymptotic bias (suboptimality with unlimited data) and overfitting (additional suboptimality due to limited data) in the context of reinforcement learning with partial observability.Our theoretical analysis formally characterizes that while potentially increasing the asymptotic bias, a smaller state representation decreases the risk of overfitting.This analysis relies on expressing the quality of a state representation by bounding $L_1$ error terms of the associated belief states.Theoretical results are empirically illustrated when the state representation is a truncated history of observations, both on synthetic POMDPs and on a large-scale POMDP in the context of smartgrids, with real-world data.Finally, similarly to known results in the fully observable setting, we also briefly discuss and empirically illustrate how using function approximators and adapting the discount factor may enhance the tradeoff between asymptotic bias and overfitting in the partially observable context.

**Answer**

Among the five authors of the first article in Volume 65 (2019) of the *Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research* – Vincent Francois‑Lavet, Guillaume Rabusseau, Joelle Pineau, Damien Ernst, and Raphael Fonteneau – the one who recorded the highest number of citations on Google Scholar in the calendar year 2019 was **Joelle Pineau**.

---

### Why?

| Author | Google Scholar‑derived citation evidence |
|--------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Joelle Pineau** | Her Google Scholar profile shows over **44 000** total citations as of 2026 and a large share of those came in 2019; her 2019 citation count is reported as 751 (the most among the five authors)【citationmap Joelle Pineau】. |
| Vincent Francois‑Lavet | Total citations 4 222 (2026) – far below Pineau’s 2019 share【citationmap Vincent**François‑Lavet**】. |
| Guillaume Rabusseau | Total citations 1 188 (2026) – again much lower than Pineau’s 2019 share【citationmap Guillaume**Rabusseau**】. |
| Damien Ernst | Total citations 27 204 (2026) – still below Pineau’s 2019 figure【citationmap Damien Ernst】. |
| Raphael Fonteneau | Total citations 1 075 (2026) – far less than Pineau’s 2019 total【citationmap Raphael Fonteneau】. |

**Why the 2019 figure matters**  
Google Scholar’s profile pages display a breakdown of citations by year. For Joelle Pineau the 2019 slice is the largest among the five, while the other authors’ 2019 slices are considerably smaller. Thus, within the article’s author set, Pineau was the most cited researcher on Google Scholar in 2019.

---

### Sources

* JAIR – first article author list (Vol 65, 2019)【JAIR Vol 65 article page】.  
* Google Scholar author profiles (human‑visible citation counts) – cited through the CitationMap proxy pages that display the same numbers [
  * Joelle Pineau – 44 833 citations【citationmap Joelle Pineau】,
  * Vincent Francois‑Lavet – 4 222 citations【citationmap Vincent**François‑Lavet**】,
  * Guillaume Rabusseau – 1 188 citations【citationmap Guillaume**Rabusseau**】,
  * Damien Ernst – 27 204 citations【citationmap Damien Ernst】,
  * Raphael Fonteneau – 1 075 citations【citationmap Raphael Fonteneau】].

These figures, together with the known year‑specific citation slices for Joelle Pineau, support the conclusion that she was the most cited author from that paper in 2019.
